title: What training does OSHA's Process Safety Management standard require?
description: What 29 CFR 1910.119 requires for operator initial and three yearly refresher training, maintenance and contractor training, and the records OSHA expects.
shortAnswer: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) Process Safety Management standard, 29 CFR 1910.119, requires every employee operating a covered process to be trained in a process overview and the operating procedures before operating it, and to receive refresher training at least every three years. Maintenance employees must be trained on process hazards and their job procedures, and contract employers must train their own workers in safe work practices and the facility's known hazards.
keyTakeaways: Paragraph (g)(1) requires initial training in a process overview and the operating procedures, with emphasis on specific safety and health hazards, emergency operations including shutdown, and safe work practices.
Paragraph (g)(2) requires refresher training at least every three years, and more often if necessary, with the frequency set in consultation with the operating employees.
Each training record must show the employee's identity, the training date, and the means used to verify the employee understood the training, for both employer and contract employees.

Training obligations also sit in mechanical integrity (j)(3) and management of change (l)(3), so operators, maintenance staff and affected contractors must be trained before a changed process restarts.
As at November 2026 the 1992 text remains in force. OSHA has been gathering input on possible revisions through a Small Business Advocacy Review Panel, but no revised standard has been issued.
regulator: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), US Department of Labor
appliesTo: Employers with processes involving a highly hazardous chemical at or above the Appendix A threshold quantity, or 10,000 pounds or more of a flammable liquid or gas, such as refineries, chemical plants, gas processing and some utility and LNG facilities
Employees involved in operating a covered process
Employees who maintain the ongoing integrity of process equipment
Contract employers and contract employees performing maintenance, repair, turnaround, major renovation or specialty work on or adjacent to a covered process

sections.heading: Which facilities and workers does the PSM training rule cover?

blocks.text: The training rules apply wherever a process is covered by [29 CFR 1910.119](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1910.119), which means a process involving a highly hazardous chemical at or above its listed threshold quantity, or a flammable liquid or gas in a quantity of 10,000 pounds or more. Within those sites, the duties fall on three groups: operators, maintenance employees, and contractors working on or next to the process.

The standard itself excludes retail facilities, oil or gas well drilling or servicing operations, and normally unoccupied remote facilities. That last exclusion matters for energy companies: a remote pipeline station or wellsite that employees only visit periodically may fall outside PSM, while a gas processing plant or refinery upstream of it does not. Federal OSHA's broader [training requirements](/regulations/osha-training-requirements) still apply where PSM does not.

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects 29 CFR 1910.119 as published in the Electronic Code of Federal Regulations as at November 2026. OSHA's PSM page describes a Small Business Advocacy Review Panel on potential revisions and a stakeholder meeting held on October 12, 2022. No revised training text has been adopted. Check the primary sources before relying on any paragraph reference.

sections.heading: What initial training must process operators receive?

blocks.text: Each employee involved in operating a process, and each employee before being involved in operating a newly assigned process, must be trained in an overview of that process and in its written operating procedures. Paragraph (g)(1)(i) states that the training "shall include emphasis on the specific safety and health hazards, emergency operations including shutdown, and safe work practices applicable to the employee's job tasks."

The phrase "newly assigned process" is the trigger most often missed. An experienced operator moving from a hydrotreater to a crude unit needs initial training on the crude unit before operating it, even though they have years of operating experience elsewhere on site. The content is anchored in the operating procedures required by paragraph (f), so the training can only be as current as those procedures.

Paragraph (g)(1)(ii) allowed one exception: for employees already operating a process on May 26, 1992, an employer could certify in writing that the employee had the required knowledge, skills and abilities instead of providing initial training. That grandfathering applies only to that cohort. Anyone hired or reassigned since then needs documented initial training.

sections.heading: How often is PSM refresher training required?

blocks.text: Refresher training must be provided at least every three years, and more often if necessary, to each employee involved in operating a process. Paragraph (g)(2) states the purpose as assuring "that the employee understands and adheres to the current operating procedures of the process", and requires the employer to set the appropriate frequency in consultation with the employees who operate the process.

Three years is therefore a ceiling, not a target. The non-mandatory Appendix C to the standard says that if evaluation shows trained employees are not at the expected level of knowledge and skill, the employer will need to revise the program, retrain, or provide more frequent refresher sessions until the deficiency is resolved. A refresher cycle set out in a [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) should record the consultation that produced it.

The same three year rhythm appears in paragraph (o), which requires employers to certify at least every three years that they have evaluated compliance with the standard. Training records are among the first documents a compliance audit team examines, so a lapsed refresher tends to surface there before an OSHA inspector finds it.

sections.heading: What training applies to maintenance staff and process changes?

blocks.text: Maintenance employees must be trained in an overview of the process and its hazards and in the procedures that apply to their job tasks. Paragraph (j)(3) requires this for each employee involved in maintaining the ongoing integrity of process equipment, so that the employee can perform the job tasks safely.

Management of change creates a separate, event driven duty. Under paragraph (l)(3), employees involved in operating a process, and maintenance and contract employees whose job tasks will be affected by a change, must be informed of and trained in the change before start-up of the process or the affected part of it. Paragraph (i) adds that the pre-startup safety review must confirm training of each operating employee has been completed for new or significantly modified facilities.

In practice this means every management of change record should name the affected roles and link to the training delivered before restart. The guide on [updating training when requirements change](/guides/how-to-update-training-when-regulations-change) describes how to identify affected roles quickly.

The contract employer trains its own employees, and the host employer must check that it does. Paragraph (h) applies to contractors performing maintenance or repair, turnaround, major renovation or specialty work on or adjacent to a covered process. It does not apply to incidental services that do not influence process safety, such as janitorial work, food and drink services, laundry, delivery or other supply services.

items: **Contract employer, (h)(3)(i) and (ii):** assure each contract employee is trained in the work practices necessary to safely perform the job, and instructed in the known potential fire, explosion or toxic release hazards related to the job and the process, and the applicable provisions of the emergency action plan.
**Contract employer, (h)(3)(iii):** document that each contract employee received and understood the training, in a record with identity, date, and the means used to verify understanding.

**Host employer, (h)(2):** obtain and evaluate the contractor's safety performance and programs, inform the contract employer of known fire, explosion or toxic release hazards, explain the emergency action plan, control entry and exit of contract employees, periodically evaluate contractor performance, and keep a contract employee injury and illness log.

blocks.text: Because the host must periodically evaluate whether contract employers meet their (h)(3) obligations, many refineries and gas plants require contractors to submit training records or complete a site orientation before badging. The site orientation alone does not satisfy (h)(3), which requires training in the work practices of the contractor's own job.

sections.heading: How do PSM training duties map to roles, frequency and audit evidence?

blocks.text: The table below is an original mapping of each PSM training clause to the role it covers, when it is due, and the evidence an OSHA compliance officer or a paragraph (o) audit team would ask to see. It is illustrative, not an OSHA template.

blocks.text: The verification column is where many programs fall short. A sign-in sheet proves attendance, not understanding. The guide to [preparing training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) covers record structures that capture the verification method alongside completion.

sections.heading: What does OSHA's appendix say good PSM training looks like?

blocks.text: OSHA's non-mandatory Appendix C advises employers to define who is trained and on which subjects, and to write learning goals in clear measurable terms before training begins. It says employers should describe the actions and conditions under which the employee will demonstrate competence and what counts as acceptable performance.

The appendix favors hands-on methods, giving the example of control room operators trained on a simulated control panel where upset conditions are displayed and the trainee works through the operating procedures to restore normal parameters. It also says the language known to trainees should be used where there is a language barrier, and that maintenance and contract employees need current training when processes change.

Energy and chemical operators that apply this guidance usually separate knowledge of the procedure from demonstrated performance of it, which is the distinction described in [verification of competency](/glossary/verification-of-competency). See how this applies across [energy and resources organizations](/industries/energy-resources).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry links each operating procedure revision to the process, the roles that operate or maintain it, and the assessment points that show understanding. When a management of change alters a procedure, the affected roles and the training that must be completed before restart can be identified from those links rather than by searching course libraries.

faqs.q: Is PSM refresher training required every year?
faqs.a: No. Paragraph (g)(2) requires refresher training at least every three years, and more often if necessary. The employer must decide the appropriate frequency in consultation with the employees who operate the process, so some sites run annual refreshers for complex or high consequence units while others use the three year maximum.

faqs.q: Does PSM require a test after training?
faqs.a: The standard does not mandate a written test, but paragraph (g)(3) requires the employer to ascertain that each operator received and understood the training and to record the means used to verify that understanding. A test, oral examination, observed walkthrough or simulator exercise can all serve, provided the method is recorded.

faqs.q: Do delivery drivers and janitorial contractors need PSM contractor training?
faqs.a: No. Paragraph (h)(1) excludes contractors providing incidental services that do not influence process safety, such as janitorial work, food and drink services, laundry, delivery or other supply services. They may still need site safety and emergency information under other OSHA standards and the facility's emergency action plan.

faqs.q: Do PSM training records have a fixed retention period?
faqs.a: Paragraph (g) does not state a retention period. It requires a record with the employee's identity, the training date and the means of verification. Because paragraph (o) compliance audits look back over three year cycles and employers must keep the two most recent audit reports, many sites retain training records for at least that long.

factCheck.claim: Paragraph (g)(1)(i) requires each employee operating a process, and each employee before operating a newly assigned process, to be trained in an overview of the process and the operating procedures, with emphasis on specific safety and health hazards, emergency operations including shutdown, and safe work practices
Paragraph (g)(1)(ii) allowed written certification in lieu of initial training for employees already operating a process on May 26, 1992
Paragraph (g)(2) requires refresher training at least every three years, and more often if necessary, with frequency determined in consultation with operating employees
Paragraph (g)(3) requires a record containing the employee's identity, the date of training, and the means used to verify understanding

Paragraph (h)(1) applies to contractors performing maintenance or repair, turnaround, major renovation or specialty work and excludes janitorial, food and drink, laundry, delivery or other supply services; (h)(3) sets contract employer training and documentation duties

Paragraph (j)(3) requires training for employees maintaining process equipment integrity, and (l)(3) requires affected operating, maintenance and contract employees to be trained in a change before start-up

Paragraph (o) requires certification of compliance evaluation at least every three years and retention of the two most recent audit reports; (a)(2) excludes retail facilities, oil or gas well drilling or servicing, and normally unoccupied remote facilities
